createdBy: code review R8, agent A (2 sites) + implementer measurement (3rd site, reachability, T-004 note)
impact: All three ASCII-`\d` regexes remain in src/codex.ts (:32-34, :40) and none use the pinned CPython digit table that src/dates.ts:45 and src/unicode-tables.ts already provide. If triggered, the divergence is on the success path: sessions fall into the excluded/undated bucket (changing totals and the frozen coverage line) or a scratchpad cwd renders as a full encoded-path row. In practice only SCRATCHPAD_RE is reachable (a real user cwd read from the rollout log); the rollout-filename and date-dir inputs are generated by codex with ASCII digits, so the practical likelihood is very low. Also carry forward the T-004 note: the ported CLI's `--since -Nd` detection regex must use the same pinned digit table, since usage.py:777 accepts Nd digits today.
resolution:
All three codex.ts regexes now use CPython's `\d` (category Nd), and the downstream slice this exposed was fixed in the same change.

REGEXES (src/codex.ts): ROLLOUT_RE, DATE_DIR_RE and SCRATCHPAD_RE are built with `new RegExp(..., "u")` from a character class derived from ND_RANGES at load. Derived, not written out, so it cannot drift from the table it mirrors — unicode-tables.ts is a generated file and was not hand-edited. Not `\p{Nd}`, for the reason src/dates.ts records: V8's Unicode database is newer than the reference CPython's (760 Nd code points vs 660), so `\p{Nd}` would accept 100 code points Python rejects as unassigned.

THE CARRY-FORWARD NOTE was already satisfied: the `--since -Nd` detection (usage.py:777) is argparse.ts's rewriteArgv -> isRelativeDays, which already used the pinned isDecimalDigit and already cited ISS-016, as does isNegativeNumber. Verified rather than assumed; no change needed.

INTERACTION FOUND AND FIXED — the reason this is not a regex-only change. Widening the regexes made a latent UTF-16 slice REACHABLE. usage.py:209 and :289 carve the date fields out of a rollout filename by POSITION (`session_file[8:18]`, `[8:12]`, `[13:15]`, `[16:18]`), and until now ROLLOUT_RE guaranteed those positions were ASCII. With astral digits admitted, `slice(8, 18)` cut a surrogate pair in half. Measured before the fix: the port produced the window key "𝟎𝟏𝟐𝟑\ud835" — ending in a lone surrogate — where CPython produces eight digits. That key selects the session's window, so it moves totals. Shipping the regex fix alone would have traded a strictness divergence for a corruption one.

pySlice (added for ISS-001) was widened from `[:n]` to the full `s[start:end]` contract and applied at all four codex sites; the ccusage call site became pySlice(res.stderr, 0, 400). The implementation is now `Array.from(s).slice(start, end).join("")` — deliberately dropping the allocation-free scan, because supporting negative indices needs the code-point count anyway and these sites run once per process or once per session file, not per cell per row like pyLen. JS Array.slice and Python slicing agree on integer bounds, negatives, and out-of-range clamping; that claim is tested rather than asserted.

TESTS (unicode-parity.test.mjs, differential vs live CPython):
1. All three regexes vs Python's, over ASCII / Arabic-Indic / Devanagari / fullwidth / Mathematical-Bold digits plus nine negatives. Corpus limited to long-assigned digits so it runs unconditionally instead of skipping on a Unicode-version mismatch the way the table drift test must.
2. A premise check that the corpus can actually distinguish ASCII `\d` from Nd — without it the comparison could pass on an ASCII corpus and prove nothing.
3. The pinned table vs V8: finds a code point V8 calls Nd and the pinned table does not (by search, not hardcoded) and asserts the port REJECTS it.
4. codexStartDate vs `name[8:18]` over ASCII, Mathematical Bold, and Arabic-Indic names, plus an explicit no-unpaired-surrogate assertion.
5. pySlice vs CPython over 44 (string, start, end) combinations covering negatives, reversed, and out-of-range bounds.

MUTATION-VERIFIED, and tests 1 and 3 proved to be separately load-bearing:
- Revert to ASCII `\d` -> test 1 fails, test 3 passes.
- Use `\p{Nd}` -> test 3 fails, test 1 passes (its corpus is deliberately limited to digits both databases agree on).
- Revert the codex slices to `.slice()` -> test 4 fails.
- Break pySlice -> 5 tests fail.

Suite: 327 unit tests (was 322), contract 19/19, parity --final 266 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped, 45/45 goldens byte-match.
title: codex.ts regexes use JS `\d` (ASCII) where Python `\d` is Unicode Nd — 3 sites, success-path totals
